A London resident has shared how she is coping with the UK's latest heatwave without air conditioning, from abandoning work-from-home days and relying on fans to eating cold meals and escaping to parks and cooler destinations.
The UK is experiencing its fifth heatwave of the summer, with temperatures making everyday activities increasingly difficult for people living in homes and offices without adequate cooling.
For London-based journalist Roya Shahidi, the heat has been particularly challenging. She describes herself as someone who struggles with both extremes, saying a breezy day of around 70°F (21°C) is her ideal weather, according to Business Insider.
The UK's highest temperature recorded so far this summer reached 101°F (38.1°C) at Kew Gardens in London on Thursday, according to the Met Office. The weather service has also said the summer is on course to become the UK's hottest on record.
While temperatures of this level are commonplace in parts of the world, the heat has proved particularly uncomfortable in Britain, where air conditioning is relatively uncommon and many buildings can retain heat.
Shahidi said the weather has forced her to rethink her normal working routine and find ways to stay cool throughout the day.
She has stopped working from home when temperatures rise
Shahidi said working from home has largely become impractical during the heatwave because her London flat can feel even hotter than the street outside.
Although she has a flexible job, she has increasingly chosen to go into the office because it has air conditioning.
Her commute is short, which makes the decision easier. However, she noted that the calculation is different for people who have to undertake longer journeys on public transport, much of which is not air-conditioned.
There is one drawback to working in the office: the air conditioning can be so strong that she needs to take a sweater with her.
Londoners are spending more time outdoors
The heat has also changed how people spend their evenings.
Shahidi told Business Insider that she has noticed more people socialising outside after work, particularly at riverside, outdoor and park-side venues.
Fans have become essential
Without air conditioning at home, Shahidi said a fan has become essential to getting through the night.
She relies on a tower fan to cool down enough to sleep, describing it as indispensable during the current weather.
She is far from alone. Fan sales reportedly increased by almost 3,000% in June, according to Currys chief executive Alex Baldock, as demand for cooling products surged during the heat.
Shahidi said she now wishes she had also bought a small electric handheld fan.
Instead, she carries a paper fan in her handbag, which has even left her with mild wrist pain from repeatedly using it.
Outdoor swimming is difficult to book
With temperatures soaring, London's outdoor pools and lidos have become another popular escape.
But demand has made getting a swimming slot difficult, particularly between 5pm and 7pm, when office workers finish for the day.
London's parks are turning brown
The heat and prolonged dry weather have also transformed the capital's green spaces.
Drought has been declared across most of England, while areas that would normally have lush green grass have begun turning dusty and brown.
The dry conditions have also changed the experience of summer festivals. Events traditionally associated with muddy fields, rain and wellington boots are now being compared with the dustier atmosphere of Burning Man.
She has stopped cooking hot meals
The heat has affected what Shahidi eats as well.
She said she normally enjoys cooking but has largely abandoned it during the heatwave because using an oven or boiling water on the hob can make her flat unbearably hot.
Instead, her summer diet has consisted largely of salads, cold food and grazing-style spreads.
Leaving London provides some relief
Another way Shahidi has tried to escape the heat is by getting out of London.
She said several of her friends have opted for staycations near the coast or outside the capital. Although temperatures remain high across much of Britain, leaving London can feel noticeably cooler.
Even ice-cold water has become a cooling tool
At home, Shahidi has resorted to a much simpler method when the heat becomes overwhelming: putting a glass of ice-cold water against her forehead.
She said she has repeatedly used the technique for immediate relief, particularly after cleaning her flat during the hottest part of the day.

Thunderstorms, Hail, and Heatwave Expected Across Morocco This Weekend
Morocco is bracing for contrasting weather conditions this weekend, with thunderstorms forecast in several provinces and temperatures reaching up to 45°C in the south.
Agadir – Thunderstorms accompanied by hail and strong wind gusts, along with high temperatures reaching 45°C, are expected in several provinces of Morocco from Saturday to Sunday, according to the General Directorate of Meteorology (DGM).
The DGM issued an orange-level alert warning of thunderstorms accompanied by hail and strong gusts of wind, with rainfall amounts ranging between 25 and 35 millimeters.
The storms are forecast for Saturday from 1 p.m. to 11 p.m. in the provinces of Ifrane, Midelt, Boulemane, Sefrou, Guercif, Taza, Driouch, Figuig, Jerada, Oujda-Angad, Taourirt, and Azilal.
The same weather conditions are expected on Sunday between 1 p.m. and 11 p.m. in Al Hoceima, Sefrou, Guercif, Taza, Taourirt, Ifrane, and Driouch.
Meanwhile, a heatwave is forecast for Saturday in several southern provinces, with temperatures expected to range between 42°C and 45°C.
The affected provinces include Oued Ed-Dahab, Tata, Boujdour, Assa-Zag, Aousserd, and Es-Semara.
The DGM’s alert comes as Morocco continues to experience significant variations in weather conditions, with thunderstorms forecast in parts of the country while extreme heat is expected in southern areas.

Heat, Dehydration and Alleged Mismanagement Mar Independence Day Events many place's in Tripura
By Our Correspondent
Agartala, August 15, 2026
Independence Day celebrations at several locations in Tripura were reportedly disrupted by heat-related illnesses on Saturday, with students, police personnel and even a parade commander falling sick amid allegations of inadequate arrangements for drinking water and medical support.
At Kulai Higher Secondary School ground in Dhalai district, DSP Amit Kumar, an IPS officer serving as the parade commander, reportedly became unwell while participating in the Independence Day programme. The incident occurred amid intense heat and prolonged exposure to the sun.
The condition of the parade commander became a major talking point at the venue, while questions were also raised over whether adequate arrangements had been made to protect personnel and students participating in the ceremonial parade from dehydration and heat exhaustion.
A similar situation was reported from Kanchanpur, where around five to seven students allegedly fell ill during the official Independence Day flag-hoisting programme. According to local accounts, several students were reportedly affected by the intense heat and dehydration and were subsequently taken to Kanchanpur Sub-Divisional Hospital for medical attention.
The incident has triggered criticism over the arrangements made for children who were brought to participate in the programme despite the prevailing hot and humid weather.
Questions have particularly been raised over the availability of drinking water at the venue. While allegations circulated that adequate arrangements were made for dignitaries, critics claimed that ordinary participants and students did not receive sufficient access to drinking water.
Meanwhile, reports from the main Independence Day programme organised by the Sepahijala district administration suggested that approximately 15–20 students and police personnel participating in the parade became unwell, with some reportedly losing consciousness because of the heat.
A medical team present at the venue reportedly provided first aid to several affected participants, while others were sent to hospital for further treatment.
The incidents have sparked a broader debate about the preparedness of government authorities for large outdoor public programmes during periods of extreme heat.
Questions over arrangements and safety
Independence Day celebrations traditionally involve large numbers of schoolchildren, police personnel, NCC members and other participants who often have to remain outdoors for extended periods. In such circumstances, adequate drinking water, shaded areas, first-aid facilities, medical teams and arrangements for rapid evacuation become essential.
The reported incidents have therefore raised questions about whether sufficient preventive measures were in place at the venues.
Critics have questioned the wisdom of organising prolonged outdoor programmes involving children and personnel under intense sunlight without ensuring adequate hydration and emergency medical support.
The incidents have also prompted public criticism of what some described as a mismatch between the scale of official celebrations and the basic facilities available to participants.

The department urged people heading to forests and picnic sites for the Assumption Day holiday to exercise particular caution and avoid any activity that could start a fire.
The public was specifically warned against lighting fires, using electrical tools capable of producing sparks or flames, and discarding cigarette butts or lit matches.
The forestry department stressed that fires for cooking are permitted only in designated barbecue areas at official picnic sites.
It also reminded the public that starting a fire is a criminal offence under forestry and wildfire prevention legislation and carries severe penalties.
Anyone who sees smoke or a fire is urged to immediately contact the forestry department on 1407 or the fire service on 112.
